text.p: Wall Street stocks staggered lower Wednesday as a sell-off in bonds sent the Dow Jones industrial average tumbling nearly 130 points.
Just after 1 p.m. EST, the Dow was off 88.80 points at 6,384.45 after recovering from a loss of 129.94 points at 6,343.31.
In the broader market, declining issues swamped advances 7-1 on active volume of 315 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index lost 13.44 to 1,299.11, and the American Stock Exchange index fell 7.74 to 583.05.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond plunged more than 1-1/4 points, raising its yield to 6.59 percent from 6.49 percent Tuesday.

"The bond market has stopped going lower in terms of yields and that's important for the stock market," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co. Higher yields make bonds more attractive relative to stocks.
The broad bond market sell-off was triggered by comments from Robert Hormats, a vice chairman at Goldman Sachs International.

In an interview broadcast on Reuters Financial Television, Hormats said he thought the rising U.S. trade imbalance posed a potential threat to dollar-based assets, which in turn could quell institutional appetite for U.S. Treasury bonds in Japan.
Wall Street was concerned that the Federal Reserve might need to raise interest rates in an effort to encourage foreign investors to continue to buy bonds.

"It doesn't mean a wholesale pullback, it doesn't mean they are going to stop buying," Hormats said. "It just means that the risk in the back of their minds goes up the longer these very large trade balances continue."

Hormats added that he remained optimistic about the stock market in the medium term, but said that an extended bond market sell-off, which would push U.S. long-term rates higher, could produce a slight correction in the market.
The suggestion that interest rates could be headed even slightly higher hit stocks hard.
Of the 30-blue-chip stocks in the Dow index, 29 posted losses at midsession. Exxon Corp. was the only component to escape losses, standing unchanged at 94.

The market also was buffeted by rumours that International Business Machines Corp. was on the verge of issuing a profit warning. IBM was off 3 at 155 despite widespread scepticism on Wall Street that such a warning would materialise.
The broad selling pressure had some analysts arguing that a psychological shift was underway on Wall Street.

"I think the psychology now is you'd better be the first one out the door," said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co. "I think a lot of professional money managers who had hoped these gains would last until Jan. 2 are scared out of their mind right now."
